hypothesis: Collapsing the memory to one representative snippet per distinct label (plus a candidate-label catalogue in the prompt) matches or beats fewshot_all's val accuracy on the label-rich datasets while cutting injected context by >50%, because duplicates of the same label carry no discriminative information and a 'choose exactly one candidate' framing yields better-formatted answers.

Keying memory on canonicalised answers (atom maps / explicit-H brackets / parenthesisation removed, fragments sorted) creates groups of behavioural duplicates; injecting a short 'resolved duplicate records' section instead of a demo bank, and short-circuiting exact duplicates without an LLM call, keeps accuracy within noise of fewshot_all with a 5-10x smaller injected context, and improves open-answer-format datasets where the same answer has many surface forms.

Prompting with mined contrastive pairs (two lexically close problems whose answers differ, plus the words that distinguish them) teaches the decision boundary rather than the output format, and therefore beats a flat demo bank on datasets with many confusable near-duplicate classes, at equal or smaller context.

The strongest baseline (fewshot_all) loses accuracy only because its demo budget is consumed in arrival order, so frequent-class duplicates and one very long record crowd out rare classes; re-ordering the SAME demos by class coverage (one representative per distinct answer, rarest first, then round-robin second exemplars, per-demo snippet clipping) and injecting ~26k chars instead of 30k will match fewshot_all on small-label tasks and beat it on label-rich long-tail tasks (USPTO: 50 distinct answers in 50 training items; LawBench: 143 distinct answers in 200 items) at ~25% less context.

In label-rich tasks the dominant error is emitting an answer surface form that never occurs in the ground truth (wrong components / separator / ordering); canonicalising answers into signatures (separator unification across ';', ',', full-width variants; component sorting; label-prefix stripping), merging all examples per signature, keeping a first/mid/last spread of exemplars per signature, and rendering a signature inventory ordered by frequency will make the legal output space explicit and beat behavioural_dedupe_cache and fewshot_all on LawBench and USPTO while staying under ~26k chars and not hurting Symptom2Disease.

A flat demo bank forces one global similarity competition over hundreds of candidates and drops answers when context runs out; building a two-level tree offline (leaves = distinct answers with exemplars, clusters = average-linkage agglomeration on answer-surface lexical similarity capped at 8-14 groups, each group prefixed by its most central 'hub' label) turns prediction into a cheap route-then-choose decision and shows the whole answer set in ~14k chars, matching fewshot_all on small-label tasks and beating it on label-rich tasks, without any extra LLM call.

When answers are long payloads that are largely edited copies of the problem text (measured: 65% of gold answer tokens already occur in the query on the retrosynthesis-style task, 51% recoverable from the 3 nearest demo answers), storing each solved case as an explicit copy/add edit tuple ('keep these verbatim fragments, introduce these new fragments') and retrieving the k nearest of those rules will beat a flat whole-record demo bank at ~1/3 the context, and will not hurt label-style tasks where the rules degenerate into short fragment statements.

The two structural losses of the strongest baseline are (a) arrival-order demos crowd out rare answers and near-duplicates, and (b) 220-char head-only clipping silently deletes the informative tail of long records. Replacing arrival order with set-cover greedy selection over demo text tokens (one guaranteed slot per distinct answer, rarest first, then marginal-coverage fill) plus head+tail straddle clipping derived from the memory's median record length, plus a one-line ANSWER VOCABULARY of every distinct answer, will match the baseline on small-label tasks and beat it on long-tail answer spaces (143 distinct answers in 200 records) at no more context.

Every stored memory system hardcodes one retrieval width, but nearest-neighbour retrieval helps exactly when answers are reusable and hurts when they are instance-unique payloads. Maintaining an online reusability prior (mean nearest-neighbour self-similarity of the memory) and switching retrieval regime from the query-to-prior ratio -- REPLICATION (few whole nearest cases, 'reuse the structure') / BREADTH (nearest cases + reserved one-per-answer slots) / REASON (wide one-per-answer category bank) -- will beat any fixed-width system on average across a mixture of instance-unique-payload, small-label and long-tail-answer tasks, with no LLM call and no per-dataset knob.
